stimulus.title: Cooling the Streets: Urban Heat Islands and Tree Canopies
stimulus.body: On a cloudless February afternoon, a dark asphalt car park in the outer suburbs can absorb so much solar radiation that its surface temperature climbs above fifty-five degrees Celsius—twenty degrees hotter than a shaded grassy park just two streets away. Scientists call this effect the Urban Heat Island: dense clusters of concrete, bitumen and dark rooftops trap warmth during the day and release it slowly after sunset, keeping night-time temperatures elevated. Expanding urban tree canopies offers one of the most cost-effective ways to cool neighbourhoods. Mature street trees act like natural umbrellas, intercepting sunlight before it strikes pavement, while also cooling the surrounding air through evapotranspiration—the release of water vapour from leaves. Field measurements across several Australian cities show that streets with at least thirty per cent canopy cover can be three to five degrees cooler at street level during heatwaves, reducing both heat stress for pedestrians and household electricity demand for air conditioning.

workedSolution: The passage names 'dense clusters of concrete, bitumen and dark rooftops.'
Exam technique: verify 'Concrete, bitumen (asphalt) and dark rooftops' directly against the passage and rule out distractors that distort scope or tone.
reviewFocus: Verify passage evidence, Australian English, and absence of defensible distractor readings.

stimulus.title: The Weaver and the Mountain Stream
stimulus.body: In a valley above the snowline lived a weaver named Kael, renowned for woollen cloaks so tightly spun that no wind could pierce them. One spring, a proud merchant arrived with a chest of silver and demanded a cloak woven in a single night. 'My ship sails at dawn,' the merchant boasted, 'and I pay double for haste.' Kael shook his head and pointed toward the mountain stream beside his cottage. 'Look at the stones in the water,' he said. 'The stream polishes them round not by rushing in a single flood, but by flowing steadily for a thousand years. If I pull the loom too fast, the threads snap or gap, and the mountain wind will find every flaw.' The merchant scoffed and rode away to hire a careless apprentice. Three weeks later, caught in a gale at sea, the merchant shivered inside his thin, uneven cloak and remembered the quiet sound of the loom.

Exam technique: verify 'His ship was sailing at dawn.' directly against the passage and rule out distractors that distort scope or tone.
reviewFocus: Verify passage evidence, Australian English, and absence of defensible distractor readings.

stimulus.title: The Weaver and the Mountain Stream
stimulus.body: In a valley above the snowline lived a weaver named Kael, renowned for woollen cloaks so tightly spun that no wind could pierce them. One spring, a proud merchant arrived with a chest of silver and demanded a cloak woven in a single night. 'My ship sails at dawn,' the merchant boasted, 'and I pay double for haste.' Kael shook his head and pointed toward the mountain stream beside his cottage. 'Look at the stones in the water,' he said. 'The stream polishes them round not by rushing in a single flood, but by flowing steadily for a thousand years. If I pull the loom too fast, the threads snap or gap, and the mountain wind will find every flaw.' The merchant scoffed and rode away to hire a careless apprentice. Three weeks later, caught in a gale at sea, the merchant shivered inside his thin, uneven cloak and remembered the quiet sound of the loom.
